doc.title: Lonnie Liston Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 9, 2021

title: Miles's studio: three keyboards and the Yamaha electric organ
summary: Credits on Miles's records; first session with three keyboards, Miles refusing the Rhodes and handing him an unfamiliar Yamaha keyboard.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: Yeah. I was reading about your time with Miles and I wondered if when those records came out that you played on if you were anxious to see if they credited you, because there was an awful lot of people involved in those things I think.

Yeah. They finally gave me credit for — I think — because they sent me, years later, “On the Corner” they gave me credit for “Ife” I think. But it was, like you say, shoot, when I first got the call to do a Miles I think they was working on something and I walked into the studio and there’s three keyboards. So I assumed that I was supposed to wait my turn. I didn’t know — because back then Miles was really experimenting. And so I was standing up against the wall and Miles walked over and said what the bleep you waiting for? And there’s Herbie on one keyboard and another pianist. And I’m saying, oh man, I never even played with another keyboard player, now there’s three of us. So I mean, Monk, I had to really listen, because you know we can’t all play the same thing, we can’t get in each other’s way. And so, and then I just learned about the Fender Rhodes when I was doing “Thembi” with Pharoah. So when I got with Miles I said oh man I’m going to really get into the Fender Rhodes. So I go to Miles’ house one day and I said, “Well Miles, where’s the Fender Rhodes?” He said, “Oh no, I’m tired of that.” Because you know he had Herbie Hancock play the Fender Rhodes, Chick Corea, Joe Zawinul. He said, “I want another sound.” And I said, “Well what am I supposed to play?” So the Japanese had just given Miles a brand new Yamaha organ, you know, but not the one like © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

Jimmy Smith, it was like a regular keyboard, electric keyboard. So he said, “I want you to play that.” So I said, “Well Miles, I never played it.” He said, “Oh that’s fantastic.” I said, “Well Miles, can I take it home and practice?” “Oh no, no, no.” So Monk, I had to learn the keyboard and play, and create on stage. But that’s what Miles wanted. He’d get mad if you didn’t come up with anything creative each night. And you know that’s hard for somebody that wants you to really create and be yourself.
